questions.question: Which section of chapter 1 explains how deep learning works using figures?
options: 1.4 Learning rules and representations from data
1.6 Understanding how deep learning works, in three figures
questions.answer: 1.6 Understanding how deep learning works, in three figures
questions.explanation: Section 1.6's title says so. 1.4 is about learning representations, 1.5 about the meaning of 'deep', 1.7 about what makes DL different.

questions.question: Section 1.10 starts on printed page 12. Which PDF page is that?
questions.answer: PDF p.36

questions.question: Where would you look to learn the prerequisites for reading this book and how to run its code?
questions.answer: 'about this book' (printed xviii, PDF p.20), especially 'Who should read this book' and 'About the code' (p.22).
questions.explanation: The contents list 'about this book' at xviii; it covers audience, road map and code.

questions.question: What does the sequence of section titles 1.10-1.12 suggest about the authors' attitude toward AI progress?
questions.answer: Cautiously optimistic: warn against short-term hype and remember past AI winters, but believe in AI's long-term promise.
questions.explanation: Inference from titles 'Beware of the short-term hype', 'Summer can turn to winter', 'The promise of AI'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the front matter on this page?
questions.answer: glossary
questions.explanation: The front-matter entries are preface, acknowledgments, about this book, about the authors and about the cover illustration; no glossary is listed.

questions.question: Have you read the preface and 'about this book' before starting chapter 1?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: They explain the book's approach and how to set up the code (p.17-22).

questions.question: According to the contents, in which section does the book introduce backpropagation?
questions.answer: 2.4 Gradient-based optimization
questions.explanation: 'Chaining derivatives: The Backpropagation algorithm' is listed under 2.4 (printed 46, PDF p.70). 2.2 is about tensors, 2.3 about operations like broadcasting, and 3.3 is about TensorFlow.

questions.question: What three subsections appear for each of TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX in chapter 3?
questions.answer: First steps with the framework; an end-to-end example (a linear classifier in the pure framework); and what makes that framework's approach unique.
questions.explanation: Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 all list these three entries; JAX adds 'Tensors in JAX' and 'Random number generation in JAX'.

questions.question: Why might the book reimplement the first MNIST example from scratch (section 2.5) right after explaining tensors and gradients?
questions.answer: So the reader sees every concept from 2.2-2.4 (tensors, tensor operations, gradients, SGD) at work in code, demystifying what Keras's high-level training does.
questions.explanation: Inference from the section titles: 'Reimplementing our first example from scratch', 'Running one training step', 'The full training loop'.

questions.question: Chapter 2 starts on printed page 16. On which PDF page is it?
questions.answer: PDF p.40.
questions.explanation: The body of this PDF is offset by 24 pages: 16 + 24 = 40.

questions.question: Looking at the list for section 2.2, can you already define rank, shape and dtype of a tensor? If not, which page would you read first?
questions.answer: Read 'Key attributes' (printed 23, PDF p.47) after the rank-by-rank introduction starting at printed 22 (PDF p.46).
questions.explanation: Self-assessment: the contents tells you where each attribute is defined.

questions.question: Which chapter 4 example uses K-fold validation, according to the contents?
questions.answer: California housing prices
questions.explanation: Section 4.3 lists 'Validating your approach using K-fold validation' (printed 129). 4.1 and 4.2 list a plain 'Validating your approach'; MNIST is chapter 2's example.

questions.question: Name the three problem types illustrated in chapter 4.
questions.answer: Binary classification (IMDb), multiclass classification (Reuters), and regression (California housing).
questions.explanation: These are the titles of sections 4.1-4.3.

questions.question: Why does the book probably discuss 'beating a common-sense baseline' as part of model evaluation?
questions.answer: Because a model's score only means something relative to what a trivial approach achieves; if you can't beat a simple baseline, the model isn't adding value.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection title in 5.2 (printed 152, PDF p.176); the theme returns in chapter 6 ('Beating a baseline') and chapter 13 (a non-ML baseline for forecasting).

questions.question: Which Reuters subsection points to a design rule about layer sizes?
questions.answer: 'The importance of having sufficiently large intermediate layers' (printed 125, PDF p.149).
questions.explanation: Listed in section 4.2.

questions.question: Can you explain the difference between the compile step and the fit method in Keras? If not, which pages will you read?
questions.answer: The compile step (printed 97, PDF p.121) and understanding the fit method (printed 100, PDF p.124).
questions.explanation: Self-assessment using the 3.6 subsection list.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a way to build Keras models in section 7.2?
questions.answer: Writing a custom callback
questions.explanation: Custom callbacks belong to 7.3 (built-in training loops). The other three are the model-building styles of 7.2.

questions.question: What are the three phases of the universal ML workflow in chapter 6?
questions.answer: Defining the task, developing a model, and deploying the model.
questions.explanation: Titles of sections 6.1-6.3.

questions.question: Why does the workflow include 'Scaling up: Developing a model that overfits' before regularizing?
questions.answer: Overfitting demonstrates the model has enough capacity to learn the data; only then does it make sense to constrain it to generalize better.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection order in 6.2, consistent with 5.3 (improving fit) preceding 5.4 (improving generalization).

questions.question: On which PDF page does 'Using callbacks' start?
questions.answer: PDF p.232 (printed 208).

questions.question: Could you explain what training versus inference means for layers like dropout? If not, note section 7.4 (PDF p.239) for review.
questions.answer: Self-assessment; 'Training vs. inference' is at printed 215, PDF p.239.
questions.explanation: The contents entry tells you where the distinction is discussed.

questions.question: Which chapter introduces residual connections and batch normalization?
questions.answer: Chapter 9: ConvNet architecture patterns
questions.explanation: Sections 9.2 and 9.3 (printed 272 and 276; PDF p.296 and p.300). The other chapters cover classification, interpretation and segmentation.

questions.question: What are the two ways of using a pretrained model listed in section 8.3?
questions.answer: Feature extraction and fine-tuning.
questions.explanation: Subsections of 8.3 at printed 256 and 264.

questions.question: Why do sections 10.2 and 10.3 have separate TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX subsections when most of the book uses backend-agnostic Keras code?
questions.answer: Because those techniques need direct gradient computations (gradient ascent on inputs, gradient of the top class), which are written with each framework's own gradient API.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection titles, consistent with chapter 3 introducing each framework's gradient mechanism.

questions.question: What is the last section of chapter 9 about?
questions.answer: Going beyond convolution: Vision Transformers (printed 282, PDF p.306).
questions.explanation: Listed as 9.6.

questions.question: Can you state, in one sentence each, what data augmentation and fine-tuning do? Use the contents to find pages to check your answer.
questions.answer: Data augmentation: printed 252 (PDF p.276). Fine-tuning: printed 264 (PDF p.288).
questions.explanation: Self-assessment guided by the contents.

questions.question: Which object detector does the book train from scratch?
questions.answer: YOLO
questions.explanation: 12.2 is 'Training a YOLO model from scratch'. RetinaNet is used pretrained (12.3), R-CNN is discussed as the two-stage family (12.1), and SAM is a segmentation model (11.3).

questions.question: What two prompt types are used with the Segment Anything Model?
questions.answer: A target point and a target box.
questions.explanation: Subsections at printed 323 and 327 (PDF p.347 and p.351).

questions.question: Why does the temperature-forecasting example start with a commonsense, non-ML baseline?
questions.answer: To know what level of performance a trivial method achieves, so that any ML model's improvement can be judged meaningfully.
questions.explanation: Inference from the subsection order in 13.2, consistent with 'Beating a baseline' in chapter 6.

questions.question: Name the three tokenization approaches listed in section 14.2.
questions.answer: Character, word and subword tokenization.
questions.explanation: Subsections 'Character and word tokenization' (387) and 'Subword tokenization' (390).

questions.question: Do you know what distinguishes a 'set' model from a 'sequence' model for text? Section 14.3 starts on which PDF page?
questions.answer: PDF p.419 (printed 395).
questions.explanation: Self-assessment; 395 + 24 = 419.

questions.question: Which pretrained LLM does the contents name for text generation in chapter 16?
questions.answer: Gemma
questions.explanation: 16.3 lists 'Text generation with the Gemma model' (printed 485). The other models are not named on this contents page.

questions.question: List the components of the Transformer that section 15.3 covers.
questions.answer: Dot-product attention, the encoder block, the decoder block, seq2seq with a Transformer, and positional embeddings.
questions.explanation: Subsections of 15.3 at printed 439-451.

questions.question: Why might the book present sequence-to-sequence learning with RNNs before the Transformer?
questions.answer: So the reader sees the limitations of the recurrent approach and understands what attention-based Transformers improve.
questions.explanation: Inference from the order 15.2 (RNN seq2seq) → 15.3 (Transformer).

questions.question: What does LoRA stand for, and in which section is it covered?
questions.answer: Low-Rank Adaptation; section 16.3 (printed 490, PDF p.514).
questions.explanation: Listed in 16.3.

questions.question: Which of RLHF, multimodal LLMs, RAG and reasoning models could you explain today? Note the PDF page of the ones you can't.
questions.answer: RLHF p.519, multimodal LLMs p.522, RAG p.525, reasoning models p.526.

questions.question: Which dataset does the diffusion-model section use, according to the contents?
questions.answer: Oxford Flowers
questions.explanation: 17.2 lists 'The Oxford Flowers dataset' (printed 520). MNIST is chapter 2, COCO chapter 12, IMDb chapters 4/14/15.

questions.question: Which subsection of 18.3 deals with keeping small gradients from vanishing in float16?
questions.answer: 'Using loss scaling with mixed precision' (printed 559, PDF p.583).
questions.explanation: The contents lists loss scaling under 18.3; the explanation of why it is needed is general knowledge, not shown on this page.

questions.question: What does the title '19.2 Scale isn't all you need' suggest about the authors' position?
questions.answer: That making models and datasets bigger is not sufficient to reach general intelligence; something more (better generalization) is needed.
questions.explanation: Inference from the title and subsections (automatons vs. intelligent agents, local vs. extreme generalization).

questions.question: Name the two techniques in 18.1 for getting the most out of your models.
questions.answer: Hyperparameter optimization and model ensembling.
questions.explanation: Listed at printed 539 and 546.

questions.question: Can you list the four limitations of deep learning named in 19.1 from memory?
questions.answer: Struggling to adapt to novelty; sensitivity to phrasing and distractors; difficulty learning generalizable programs; the risk of anthropomorphizing models.
questions.explanation: Self-check against the 19.1 entries.

questions.question: Which approach does section 19.4 propose blending with deep learning?
questions.answer: Program synthesis
questions.explanation: 19.4 lists 'Blending deep learning and program synthesis' (printed 590). The other options are not named on this page.

questions.question: Which benchmarks or competitions related to ARC appear in section 19.3?
questions.answer: The ARC Prize (printed 581) and ARC-AGI 2 (printed 583).
questions.explanation: Both are 19.3 subsections.

questions.question: According to the 19.3 headings, what do the authors consider the essence of intelligence?
questions.answer: Abstraction acquisition and recombination.
questions.explanation: The heading reads 'The essence of intelligence: Abstraction acquisition and recombination' (printed 578).

questions.question: Name the three ways to stay up to date recommended in 20.4.
questions.answer: Practicing on Kaggle, reading arXiv, and exploring the Keras ecosystem.
questions.explanation: Subsections of 20.4 (printed 607-608).

questions.question: After finishing the book, can you explain each item in 20.1 (approaches to AI, what makes DL special, enabling technologies, the workflow, key architectures)? Use PDF pp.620-624 to check.
questions.answer: Self-assessment against section 20.1.
questions.explanation: 20.1 starts at printed 595 (PDF p.619) with its subsections at 596-600.
